processing: A tea plant cultivar rather than a finished tea. For black tea it goes through withering, rolling, full oxidation and drying as Dian Hong.
harvest_season: Depends on the tea made from it. One documented lot was picked in late March.
appearance_dry: As black tea, typically sturdy dark strands of large leaf with some gold.
appearance_liquor: As black tea, typically a clear deep orange-red.
appearance_wet: Typically large, thick leaves turning coppery, as with Yunnan large-leaf black teas.
taste_profile: One black tea made purely from it is malty, fruity and tangy with mineral notes, a long finish and a hint of rose, and less sweet than some other Dian Hong.

brewing.notes: Western-style steeping works well for black tea from this plant. Gongfu drinkers should use short pours, as large-leaf tea extracts strongly.

vintage_note: The cultivar is not sold under a year of its own: what you buy is a tea made from it, dated by that tea's harvest. Black teas from it are normally sold by the current year, with early spring picks prized.
description:
Fengqing Dayezhong is a large-leaf tea plant from Fengqing county in Yunnan, listed among the good varieties of Yunnan large-leaf tea alongside Mengku, Menghai and Jingdong types. You will mostly see it named on the label of a black tea.

It is the plant behind much of the Dian Hong story, though little detailed description of this variety on its own is easy to come by. What is said of Yunnan large-leaf tea in general applies: more polyphenols and caffeine than small-leaf plants, and best suited to pu-erh and black tea.

A single-cultivar black tea from it shows malt, fruit and tang with a stony edge and a floral finish. Other teas from it will differ with picking and process.

If a label names it, ask whether the whole lot really is this plant and from Fengqing, as the name is easy to attach and hard to check by taste alone.
history:
Yunnan large-leaf tea as a group was among the first 30 national tea cultivars recognised in China, in November 1984. Fengqing Dayezhong is listed as one of its good varieties, but its own registration details and breeding history are little documented.

Its county is where Feng Shaoqiu made his trial black tea in 1938, from local one-bud-two-leaf material, when the place was still called Shunning.
